newsitem.title: UK: All to play for in UK Conservative leadership race.
newsitem.headline: All to play for in UK Conservative leadership race.

text.p: The race to succeed former prime minister John Major as leader of Britain's main opposition Conservative party was still wide open on Tuesday after an inconclusive first ballot.
Former finance minister Kenneth Clarke came top of the ballot of the party's 164 members of parliament, winning 49 votes. But, as expected, he fell well short of outright victory.
Second place went to youthful former Welsh secretary William Hague, 36, who polled 41 votes.

In third was right-wing Euro-sceptic John Redwood, who resigned from the cabinet in June 1995 to mount an unsuccessful challenge to Major's leadership. He did better than many pundits had expected by winning 27 votes.

Both Clarke and Hague said they were confident of ultimate victory, but MPs said everything would depend on whether the two right-wing candidates who trailed in last pulled out of the second ballot, which will take place on June 17.
Bookmakers William Hill immediately made Clarke 4-5 favourite to succeed Major, followed by Hague on 5-4 and Redwood at 6-1.
A simple majority of 83 votes will be needed in the second round of voting. If there is no winner, the two front-runners will slug it out in a third ballot two days later.

"I am very encouraged by the breadth of the support I have attracted, which is much stronger than I dared to expect when this campaign started," said Clarke, who also topped a consultative poll of Conservative activists.
Clarke is the most experienced of the five candidates, but his pro-European views mean he cannot be sure of gathering the support of right-wingers in the second round.
"The Conservative Party should now unite to fight Labour. I intend to seek to broaden my appeal further by setting out how I intend to lead this party on an inclusive basis," he said.
Hague said his score had exceeded his expectations.

"I think it puts me in a very good position to campaign for the second ballot on a platform of uniting the party and giving the party a fresh start, and I think it clearly puts me in a position to win. So we will go into the second ballot with great confidence," he said.
Redwood, a fierce opponent of closer European integration, appealed to Lilley and Howard to rally to his banner.
"They will find me very generous. I want them on side and I would like them to bring as many supporters as possible.
"I believe there is a majority in the party for the kind of views I'm putting forward. They're not extreme right views... and I wish now to appeal across the party," Redwood said.
But Lord Jeffrey Archer, a Lilley supporter, said Redwood's narrow margin ahead of the other right-wing candidates meant nothing was certain.
"I don't think it's inevitable anybody will back anybody," he said.
